power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: What divides the political left from the right?
The common labels suggest progress on the left (progressives) and conserving on the right (conservatives), yet political psychology has named fear of threat as the dominant motive on the right.
Building on the ternary goal model, we pit the goal to conserve (maintenance) against the goal to reduce threat (protection).
We analyze six decades of party platforms from eleven democracies, citizens' own political goals in six countries, and citizens' judgments of party statements.
The divide is better described as one between progress (improving the present) and maintenance (keeping what is valued).
Concern with threat marks neither side.
It rises among those in opposition and at the ideological extremes.
Psychologists have long asked whether distinct motives underlie the difference between the political left and right.
The question goes back to Adorno, Frenkel-Brunswik, Levinson, and Sanford's work on the authoritarian personality (1), a type susceptible to fascism.

Later research extended the approach to political conservatism in general (2, 3) and linked it to a range of dispositions, including dogmatism (4), need for structure or closure (5, 6), fear of uncertainty (3), fear of death (7), resistance to change, and a tendency to justify the system (8, 9; for a review, see ref. 10).
text.formatted: Later research extended the approach to political conservatism in general <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3)</ref> and linked it to a range of dispositions, including dogmatism (4), need for structure or closure <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6)</ref>, fear of uncertainty (3), fear of death <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>, resistance to change, and a tendency to justify the system <ref type="bibr">(8, 9;</ref> for a review, see ref. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref>).

text.text: These accounts found a common frame in binary models of motivation, which distinguish approach from avoidance (11) and a promotion from a prevention focus (12).
text.formatted: These accounts found a common frame in binary models of motivation, which distinguish approach from avoidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref> and a promotion from a prevention focus <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: Studies in this tradition reported the right to be more avoidant and prevention-focused, and the left more approach-oriented and promotion-focused (10, 13, 14).
text.formatted: Studies in this tradition reported the right to be more avoidant and prevention-focused, and the left more approach-oriented and promotion-focused <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14)</ref>.

text.text: Further support came from physiological and neural measures: people on the right were found to show larger startle and skin-conductance responses to threatening stimuli (15), to attend more to negative stimuli (16), and to differ from those on the left in brain structure (17).
text.formatted: Further support came from physiological and neural measures: people on the right were found to show larger startle and skin-conductance responses to threatening stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>, to attend more to negative stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>, and to differ from those on the left in brain structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref>.

text.text: More recent evidence has weakened this picture.

Large studies, several of them preregistered, failed to replicate the physiological and behavioral findings (18) (19) (20) (21) and found the difference in brain structure to be much weaker than first reported (22).
text.formatted: Large studies, several of them preregistered, failed to replicate the physiological and behavioral findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(20)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21)</ref> and found the difference in brain structure to be much weaker than first reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref>.

text.text: A large cross-national study found that whether threat predicts conservatism depends on the kind of threat, the political domain, and the country (23; see also refs. 24 and 25).
text.formatted: A large cross-national study found that whether threat predicts conservatism depends on the kind of threat, the political domain, and the country (23; see also refs. <ref type="bibr">24 and 25)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, attempts to map the left-right divide onto individual differences in psychological dispositions have yielded modest results (26, 27).
text.formatted: More broadly, attempts to map the left-right divide onto individual differences in psychological dispositions have yielded modest results <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27)</ref>.

text.text: Even the most robust personality correlate-lower openness to experience among conservatives-is small (meta-analytic r ≈ -.15 to -.18), weaker outside Western countries, and may partly reflect politics shaping how people describe themselves (28) (29) (30) (31).
text.formatted: Even the most robust personality correlate-lower openness to experience among conservatives-is small (meta-analytic r ≈ -.15 to -.18), weaker outside Western countries, and may partly reflect politics shaping how people describe themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(30)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(31)</ref>.

text.text: Liberals and conservatives thus appear more alike in their psychological makeup than different (27, 32).
text.formatted: Liberals and conservatives thus appear more alike in their psychological makeup than different <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these results suggest that the distinction between approach and avoidance fits the left-right divide less well than previously thought, and that stable psychological differences between left and right are smaller than long assumed.
We address this difficulty in two ways.
First, we reconsider which goal characterizes the right, and then the level at which goals are observed.
The binary scheme assigns approach to the left and avoidance to the right.
For the left the assignment seems straightforward, since it matches how liberal and progressive thinkers have described left ideology, as a pursuit of progress (33, 34).
text.formatted: For the left the assignment seems straightforward, since it matches how liberal and progressive thinkers have described left ideology, as a pursuit of progress <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(33,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34)</ref>.

text.text: For the right the matter is less settled.
It is an open question whether conservative thinking is better described as avoiding a negative future or as preserving a valued present.
Importantly, the latter is how conservative thinkers have described their own position.
In its literal sense, to conserve is to hold on to what exists.

The term acquired its political meaning in 1789, when the seating of the French National Assembly put those who supported the existing order on the right and those who would revolutionize it on the left (35, 36).
text.formatted: The term acquired its political meaning in 1789, when the seating of the French National Assembly put those who supported the existing order on the right and those who would revolutionize it on the left <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36)</ref>.

text.text: Edmund Burke, widely regarded as the founder of modern conservatism, responded to the revolution with a call for "a disposition to preserve" (37).
text.formatted: Edmund Burke, widely regarded as the founder of modern conservatism, responded to the revolution with a call for "a disposition to preserve" <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(37)</ref>.

text.text: He portrayed society as something grown over generations, in the manner of a living organism, and sustained by ongoing processes that radical change would disrupt.

Oakeshott described the conservative disposition in the same spirit, as the preference for "the actual to the possible" (38). Scruton (39) carried the idea as far as environmental conservation, which he presented as an expression of the same conservative motive: stewardship of what one has inherited.
text.formatted: Oakeshott described the conservative disposition in the same spirit, as the preference for "the actual to the possible" <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(38)</ref>. <ref type="bibr">Scruton (39)</ref> carried the idea as far as environmental conservation, which he presented as an expression of the same conservative motive: stewardship of what one has inherited.

text.text: Whether these self-descriptions reveal or conceal the actual character of conservatism, they name a goal that the binary scheme of approach and avoidance (11, 12) cannot represent.
text.formatted: Whether these self-descriptions reveal or conceal the actual character of conservatism, they name a goal that the binary scheme of approach and avoidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12)</ref> cannot represent.

text.text: Psychology has more recently begun to recognize this goal as a third category.

In lifespan research, Freund and colleagues distinguished an orientation toward maintenance from orientations toward growth and toward the prevention of loss, to describe how goals shift with age (40, 41).
text.formatted: In lifespan research, Freund and colleagues distinguished an orientation toward maintenance from orientations toward growth and toward the prevention of loss, to describe how goals shift with age <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41)</ref>.

text.text: The ternary goal model makes the general case (42, 43).
text.formatted: The ternary goal model makes the general case <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43)</ref>.

text.text: It proposes that goals in any domain are of three basic types: progress goals (seeking to change the current state for the better), protection goals (seeking to eliminate or reduce a threat), and maintenance goals (seeking to sustain a valued current state).
Empirical work has borne out the distinction in people's daily lives (44), in how goals are experienced (45, 46), and in how leaders are judged (47).
text.formatted: Empirical work has borne out the distinction in people's daily lives <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(44)</ref>, in how goals are experienced <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(45,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46)</ref>, and in how leaders are judged <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(47)</ref>.

text.text: The third category thereby separates two goals that binary models risk conflating: protection is a response to threat, whereas maintenance is pursued independently of threat, responding to a valued current state.
With this distinction, the open question becomes testable.
The stasis attributed to the right may reflect protection, as the threat account holds, or maintenance, as conservative thinkers have described it.
The second way in which we address this difficulty is to reconsider the level of analysis.
The dispositional approach treats a psychological construct as a stable property of the person, measured in general terms through questionnaires or laboratory tasks (48).
text.formatted: The dispositional approach treats a psychological construct as a stable property of the person, measured in general terms through questionnaires or laboratory tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(48)</ref>.

text.text: A different view holds that people are characterized as much by how they respond in particular settings (49) depending on the goal a proposal expresses.
text.formatted: A different view holds that people are characterized as much by how they respond in particular settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(49)</ref> depending on the goal a proposal expresses.

text.text: This approach is high in ecological validity, because it captures left-right differences as they are expressed and received in real political settings rather than inferred from reactions in the laboratory (50, 51).
text.formatted: This approach is high in ecological validity, because it captures left-right differences as they are expressed and received in real political settings rather than inferred from reactions in the laboratory <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(50,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">51)</ref>.

text.text: In summary, we contrast two accounts of the left-right divide.
The two accounts agree about the left, where both expect progress orientation, but part over the right, where the established account expects protection and the alternative maintenance.
The disagreement can be tested wherever political goals are voiced.
Top-down, in party platforms, the right should stand out from the left by its protection orientation on the established account, and by its maintenance orientation on the alternative.
Bottom-up, the same contrast applies to the goals that citizens on the left and right express in their own words.

Where the two meet, in citizens' support for party statements, the right should be drawn to protection-oriented statements on the established account, and to maintenance-oriented statements on the alternative.

We additionally ask what protection orientation follows if it does not mark the right, and examine whether it varies with a party's place in government or opposition, and with a party's or a citizen's distance from the center of the spectrum.
To measure goal orientation in political language, we trained a supervised classifier that scores any statement on the three orientations as continuous, co-occurring dimensions.
Training labels came from 2,998 statements from platforms, manifestos, and speeches in five languages, rated by 558 nativespeaking raters.
After screening raters and statements for rating quality, 1,707 statements with consistent ratings were used (Materials and Methods; SI Appendix, sections S1-S6).
The classifier pairs a frozen multilingual sentence encoder with a small trained head, so that one model scores English, German, Dutch, Polish, and Hebrew on a common scale.
On held-out statements it agreed with human raters at r = .60, .61, and .54 for progress, maintenance, and protection.
This is acceptable, given a ceiling of about .7-.8 set by the reliability of the human ratings.
See SI Appendix, section S6, for further validation, including a preregistered test.

We scored 723,918 sentences from 892 party platforms in 11 countries in the Manifesto Corpus (52), and analyzed the scores in multilevel models with sentences nested in platforms, parties, and countries.
text.formatted: We scored 723,918 sentences from 892 party platforms in 11 countries in the Manifesto Corpus <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(52)</ref>, and analyzed the scores in multilevel models with sentences nested in platforms, parties, and countries.

text.text: All differences reported below are comparisons within country (Materials and Methods; SI Appendix, section S7).

Over the six decades of the corpus, platforms became more progress-oriented and somewhat less maintenance-oriented: progress orientation rose by 0.09 points per decade on the 0-10 scale (95% CI 0.03 to 0.14, P = .008) and maintenance orientation fell by 0.03 (-0.05 to -0.01, P = .007).
Protection orientation showed no reliable trend (+0.02, P = .11; SI Appendix, section S7.1).
Two of the three trends were non-linear, those for progress and protection (Fig. 1; SI Appendix, Table S6a).
text.formatted: Two of the three trends were non-linear, those for progress and protection (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>; SI Appendix, Table <ref type="table">S6a</ref>).

text.text: The same broad patterns held within each country: Parties have come to write more about changing the present and slightly less about keeping it (SI Appendix, Fig. S1).
text.formatted: The same broad patterns held within each country: Parties have come to write more about changing the present and slightly less about keeping it (SI Appendix, Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S1</ref>).

text.text: More important for our predictions, left and right differed as the maintenance account expects.
Platforms of right-wing party families were more maintenance-oriented than those of left-wing families in the same country (0.13 points, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.21, P < .001, estimated at the year 2000).
text.formatted: Platforms of right-wing party families were more maintenance-oriented than those of left-wing families in the same country (0.13 points, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.21, P < .001, estimated at the year 2000).

text.text: For progress orientation, the difference between right and left was not reliable when estimated at the year 2000 (-0.10, P = .13), but it changed over time (-0.06 per decade, P = .018).

The two sides did not differ in 1970 (+0.06, P = .54), and by 2020 right-wing platforms were less progress-oriented (-0.22, 95% CI -0.38 to -0.05, P = .017), because progress orientation rose more than twice as fast among left-wing platforms.
Protection orientation did not differ between the two at any point (-0.05 in 2000, P = .30) (Fig. 1; SI Appendix, Table S6).
text.formatted: Protection orientation did not differ between the two at any point (-0.05 in 2000, P = .30) (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>; SI Appendix, Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>).

text.text: Relative to the variation between platforms (SD = 0.47 for maintenance and 0.51 for progress), the maintenance difference in 2000 amounts to about 0.3 SD and the progress difference in 2020 to about 0.4 SD.
Protection orientation followed political position.

Opposition parties were more protectionoriented than governing parties of the same country (0.13, 0.09 to 0.16, P < .001), on the left and on the right alike, with no interaction between incumbency and side on any orientation (SI Appendix, Table S7).
text.formatted: Opposition parties were more protectionoriented than governing parties of the same country (0.13, 0.09 to 0.16, P < .001), on the left and on the right alike, with no interaction between incumbency and side on any orientation (SI Appendix, Table <ref type="table">S7</ref>).

text.text: Governing parties, in turn, were more maintenance-oriented (0.16, 0.12 to 0.21, P < .001) and more progress-oriented (0.13, 0.04 to 0.22, P = .009).
text.formatted: Governing parties, in turn, were more maintenance-oriented (0.16, 0.12 to 0.21, P < .001) and more progress-oriented (0.13, 0.04 to 0.22, P = .009).

text.text: The predicted difference between right and left held with incumbency taken into account: right-wing platforms, in government and in opposition alike, were more maintenance-oriented (+0.11, P = .003) and less progress-oriented (-0.15, P = .027).

Finally, we asked whether the extremes of the spectrum differ from its center, using the categorical measure again: the Socialist and Nationalist families, the two at the poles, were contrasted with all other classified families.

Platforms of the pole families were more protection-oriented than those of other families in the same country (0.16, 0.07 to 0.24, P < .001) and less progress-and maintenanceoriented (-0.22, P = .040, and -0.16, P = .013) (SI Appendix, Table S8).
text.formatted: Platforms of the pole families were more protection-oriented than those of other families in the same country (0.16, 0.07 to 0.24, P < .001) and less progress-and maintenanceoriented (-0.22, P = .040, and -0.16, P = .013) (SI Appendix, Table <ref type="table">S8</ref>).

text.text: Across the corpus, then, protection language marks parties that regard their position as precarious, in opposition or at the edge of the spectrum, rather than parties of the right.
Within countries the differences were less precise but pointed the same way.
Right-wing platforms were more maintenance-oriented than left-wing platforms everywhere but in Canada, reliably so in Germany and the Netherlands.
They were reliably less progress-oriented in Israel, the Netherlands, and Canada, with no reliable difference elsewhere.
Protection orientation did not differ between right and left except in Poland, where it was higher on the right, and in Ireland, where it was higher on the left.

Incumbency was more uniform: governing parties were more maintenance-oriented and less protectionoriented than opposition parties in every country, and more progress-oriented everywhere but in Israel (SI Appendix, section S7.5 and Fig. S3).
text.formatted: Incumbency was more uniform: governing parties were more maintenance-oriented and less protectionoriented than opposition parties in every country, and more progress-oriented everywhere but in Israel (SI Appendix, section S7.5 and Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">S3</ref>).

text.text: We asked citizens in six countries to describe, in their own words, the goals they wanted their country to pursue in the coming years, and scored their answers with the same classifier (United States, n = 482; Germany, 449; Poland, 300; the Netherlands, 306; the United Kingdom, 398; Canada, 398; total n = 2,333; SI Appendix, section S9).
All six studies were preregistered with the directional hypotheses that maintenance orientation rises and progress orientation falls with conservatism, with no directional prediction for protection.
The Polish preregistration additionally specified the test of whether protection is elevated at both extremes.

For each orientation, standardized within country, we fitted a linear mixed model relating it to left-right self-placement, with random intercepts and random slopes for country, so that the pooled association is tested against its variation across the six countries.

Progress orientation decreased with self-placement toward the right (slope -0.21 points of ideology per SD, 95% CI -0.31 to -0.12, P = .002), and the association did not differ reliably between countries (P = .13).

Maintenance orientation tended to increase with conservatism, but not reliably (mixed-model slope 0.11 points of ideology per SD, -0.02 to 0.25, P = .09), and the association varied between countries (P = .016).

The slope was reliable (0.14, 0.03 to 0.26, P = .024) when institutional trust, which is lower on the right in five of the six countries and itself predicts maintenance orientation, was held constant.
This control was preregistered in every study but the Polish one, to test whether lower trust on the right masks the association between maintenance and political ideology.

We examined whether conservative ideology reflects a wish to maintain a valued present, as conservative thinkers have held, or a need to protect against threat, as psychology has explained it.
In what parties promise, in what citizens ask for, and in what citizens are willing to support, the answer was the same.
Right-wing platforms were more maintenance-oriented than left-wing platforms and increasingly less progress-oriented.

Citizens who placed themselves on the right wrote less about progress and, up to the moderate right, more about maintenance, and policy statements framed as progress won the left while statements framed as maintenance won the right.
Protection orientation separated nobody along that axis.
Where it varied with politics, it followed position rather than ideology: parties in opposition, parties at the poles of the spectrum, and citizens at either end of the scale.
Conservative thinkers from Burke onward have described their project as stewardship rather than fear (37), and the language of parties and citizens bears them out.

text.text: Moreover, the finding that only some threats, in some domains and countries, correlate with conservatism ( 23) is expected if protection orientation is a situational response rather than an ideological trait, one that intensifies when a group, of whatever stripe, perceives its position as precarious.
text.formatted: Moreover, the finding that only some threats, in some domains and countries, correlate with conservatism ( <ref type="formula">23</ref>) is expected if protection orientation is a situational response rather than an ideological trait, one that intensifies when a group, of whatever stripe, perceives its position as precarious.

text.text: The incumbency and extremity results sharpen the point: protection language belongs to whoever is in opposition, left as well as right, and to the margins of the spectrum, while maintenance language belongs to whoever governs, and conservatism adds a further increment of maintenance on top of that.
These findings may also point to where research on ideology took a wrong turn.
Adorno et al. (1) set out to describe a personality susceptible to fascism, not the political right, and they distinguished it from ordinary conservatism.
text.formatted: Adorno et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref> set out to describe a personality susceptible to fascism, not the political right, and they distinguished it from ordinary conservatism.

text.text: Later research drew on this work in addressing conservatism in general (3, 10).
text.formatted: Later research drew on this work in addressing conservatism in general <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10)</ref>.

text.text: That extension may have rested on the assumption that what is found at the extreme is present in milder form among moderates, so that the right differs from its far end only in degree.
Our data suggest a difference in kind: the moderate right was marked by maintenance, and the extremes by protection.
The original, narrower claim may thus have been closer to the mark than its generalization.
The two sides of the axis were not symmetric among citizens.
Progress orientation tracked the left more consistently than maintenance orientation tracked the right, and the maintenance slopes varied across countries whereas the progress slopes did not.
Maintenance orientation also followed a curve, highest among moderate conservatives and lower at the far right, which a linear slope understates.
Policy support showed the same asymmetry: progress framing divided left from right in five of the six samples, maintenance framing in three.

One interpretation is that the wish to maintain depends on the present in a way the wish for progress does not: progress can be wanted from any starting point, whereas maintenance is tied to evaluations of the present order and should attract conservatives more where they regard that order as theirs to keep.

Consistent with this, the maintenance difference was steadier in party platforms, where six decades average over the circumstances of single elections: right-wing platforms were more maintenance-oriented than left-wing platforms throughout.
These results open directions for future research.
One concerns what becomes of the wish to maintain where the right does not regard the present order as its own.
It may turn toward a past order to be restored, in line with the stronger focus on the past in the language of the right (53) (54) (55) (56) (57).
text.formatted: It may turn toward a past order to be restored, in line with the stronger focus on the past in the language of the right <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(53)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(54)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(55)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(56)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(57)</ref>.

text.text: Whether such past-focused language expresses maintenance, or instead protection against a present experienced as loss, cannot be told from our measure.
The lower maintenance orientation of parties at the poles is consistent with the protection reading but does not test it.
Classifying statements jointly by temporal focus (54) and by goal orientation would separate the two.
text.formatted: Classifying statements jointly by temporal focus <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(54)</ref> and by goal orientation would separate the two.

text.text: Another direction is to test directly whether maintenance orientation depends on regarding the present order as one's own, by following the same parties and voters as they move between government and opposition.
The role of institutional trust points to a further direction.
The linear association between conservatism and maintenance orientation was reliable only when institutional trust was held constant, and trust was lower on the right in most countries.
Conservatism is commonly associated with the defense of established institutions, yet many on the right today distrust the institutions that exist.
Our classifier scores whether a statement aims at maintenance, not what is to be maintained.
Coding the objects of maintenance in the same texts would give a fine-grained picture of what the left and the right each want to keep.
For the right, it would show whether the wish to maintain is directed at existing institutions, at a way of life, or at an order felt to have been lost.
Some limitations should also be noted.
The associations of goal orientations with ideology were small throughout, in party platforms, in citizens' goals, and in policy support.
Those for progress were consistent across countries and samples, whereas those for maintenance among citizens varied in size and sometimes in sign, and followed a curve across the ideological scale.
The classifier's agreement with human raters leaves measurement error that attenuates every effect reported here, and the true associations are likely larger.
All participant samples are nonprobability samples recruited online, which limits population inference, though the platform corpus is a census of the parties concerned.
The map of political motivation that emerges is a single axis running from the wish to keep things as they are to the wish to make them otherwise.
Protection is not a pole of that axis.
It is a goal that stands beside the axis and can side with either end, with a right that sees its institutions under attack or with a left that sees its gains about to be reversed.
Its political color at any moment may depend on who feels endangered.
Seen this way, left and right pursue two constructive aims, improving what does not work and keeping what does, and a society needs both.

Goal-orientation scores came from a supervised classifier: a frozen multilingual sentence encoder (multilingual-e5-large-instruct) (58) with a small trained head, a prototype-anchored attention layer and a three-layer perceptron, that predicts mean human ratings of progress, maintenance, and protection orientation on a 0-1 scale.

Training labels came from ten rating studies of party-platform statements, manifesto sentences, and political speeches in five languages, each statement rated in the original language by three to twelve raters recruited on Prolific.

Raters with low agreement, straightlining, or excessive speed were excluded, as were statements with fewer than three remaining raters or with ratings split across the scale midpoint, leaving 1,707 statements, split 60/20/20 within source.
Training was repeated over four random seeds, retaining the run with the highest mean held-out correlation (held-out r = .60, .61, .54, n = 342; cross-seed means .55, .57, .57).
In a preregistered knowngroups validation (AsPredicted #317280) of predicted differences between policy domains within parties, 12 of the 14 testable predictions were confirmed.
Some of the statements rated in the policy-support studies were also training statements (SI Appendix, section S9.5).
Architecture, training, screening, and validation are detailed in SI Appendix, sections S1-S6.

Each orientation was analyzed in a sentence-level linear mixed model (lme4/lmerTest) with sentences nested in platforms, parties, and countries.

The models included random intercepts at each of these levels, random slopes for time at the party and country levels, and, for each predictor that varied within country, a random slope at the country level.
Party-level predictors were split into their within-country and betweencountry components, and the differences reported are within country.
Each model started from this full random-effects structure and was reduced by a fixed step-down rule when a fit was singular or did not converge, so the structure retained differs between outcomes.
Satterthwaite degrees of freedom and tbased confidence intervals are reported.
Fig 1 and the tests of non-linear change come from sentencelevel generalized additive mixed models (mgcv) with the same fixed effects and smooths of year.
Step-down logs, platform-level robustness checks, and the additive models are detailed in SI Appendix, section S7.
Citizen Studies.

Six online surveys used nonprobability (opt-in) samples recruited through Prolific, screened for country of residence and first language: Poland (n = 300, June 2026), the United States (n = 482, July 2026), Germany (n = 449, July 2026), the Netherlands (n = 306), the United Kingdom (n = 398), and Canada (n = 398), the last three in September-October 2026.

Participants wrote 3-5 sentences on the most important issues facing their country (over the next ten years in the Dutch, British, and Canadian studies) and how politicians should address them; the text was scored by the classifier.
Ideology was self-placement on a 7-point left-right scale.
Institutional trust was measured with a six-item 0-10 scale (European Social Survey items; ANES items in the United States).

Six policysupport studies (United States 2008 platforms, n = 487, and United States 2012 platforms, n = 489, fielded October-November 2023, 28 statements per participant from a pool of 140; Israel 2022 platforms, n = 501, May 2026, PanelView, 12 statements per participant from a pool of 240; and the Polish, United States, and German samples above, which rated 24, 12, and 28 statements respectively) presented platform statements with party source removed for support ratings on 7-point scales.
All participants gave informed consent.
Models are specified in Results and in SI Appendix, section S9.
Preregistration and Open Science.

All nine participant studies and the classifier validation were preregistered on AsPredicted: the 2012 and 2008 platform studies (#148828, #152371; October-November 2023), the Israeli (#290163), Polish (#296975), United States (#301048), and German (#301531) studies (May-July 2026), the Dutch (#312243), Canadian (#312244), and British (#312246) studies (September 2026), and the known-groups validation of the classifier (#317280; October 2026).
